then.text: Gillian Mackie, Nessie Knitwear and Cards. Tea cosies, woolly monsters, and the finest scalloped-edge postcards in the Highlands.
A photograph of the monster? Never heard of it. I print my own cards, you know. Very good stock. Cream. Scalloped. Everyone comments.
I haven't been near the loch in weeks. Weeks. Just so you know. I wasn't asked, but I'm telling you.

else.text: Woolly monster? Tea cosy? Both? I do a bundle.

then.text: Plastic wood and brass wire? The only one who buys that together is... hold on. Let me check the till roll.
Plastic wood, brass wire, one tin of grey paint, same day, cash. 'G. Mackie.' She said it was for a nativity scene. In August.

else.text: Plastic wood? We sell plenty. Come back with a reason and I'll go through the till.
Nails, screws, hooks, hinges. All sold by the pound and the opinion.

kessock_works.text: Sorry, the Kessock Bridge is shut for resurfacing. The whole thing. Both carriageways. I know.
We'll be done once the Frost Stone's been won up at the ice rink. Don't ask how the two are connected. It's a council thing.

rail_guard.text: Inverness Station, the northern end of the line. The Kyle line goes west to the sea, the Far North line goes up to Thurso, and the sleeper train goes all the way to London. Most of these trains have a view you'll talk about for a week.
Hop aboard. The Wildlore rail runs to any town you have visited in Great Britain. Where to?

then.text: Come in out of the rain, please, but quietly. The bells are resting and the pigeons are not.
Evensong soon. The red stone glows at this hour, and it almost looks like it got its spires after all.

verger.text: St Andrew's was built in the 1860s with a red stone front and two towers that never got their spires. It has a great ring of bells, a labyrinth path in the garden and a visitor who once asked if the cathedral was real. It is.
Please keep your voice down, we're a little shy. The pigeons, however, are not.

then.text: That's a fine kilt. Wear it with a straight back and nobody will mention the draught.
Raining? That's why we've a roof. Best place in Inverness for staying dry and buying fudge.
Lovely day! Everyone's outside, so I've the market to myself. Me, the fudge and the woolly coo.
Closing up soon. If you want tablet, now's the time. After six it's just me eating it.

market_trader.text: {greeting} Tablet, shortbread, fudge, and a Highland coo made of wool. Not that kind of coo, the other one. Well, also that kind.
The Victorian Market's been selling since 1870. The roof's been up longer than I have, and it's the more waterproof of the two of us.

then.text: Fog on the Firth. The dolphins are out there, I can hear them blowing. I just can't see a single fin.
Flat calm and sunny, perfect for spotting fins. Bring a piece and a flask. The dolphins keep their own time.
Too choppy in this wind. Every wave looks like a dolphin. Every dolphin looks like a wave.

dolphin_watcher.text: The dolphins come in with the tide, so I check the tide tables like other people check the football results. High water at Chanonry is the kick-off.
Our dolphins are bottlenose. They're among the biggest in the world, because the Firth is cold, and a bigger body keeps the heat in. They are, in other words, wearing a very good jumper.

then.text: In the fog the castle looks even more like it's judging you. Don't worry, it judges everyone.
The castle gets floodlit at dusk. It goes all pink and dramatic. It knows exactly what it's doing.

castle_walker.text: That's Flora MacDonald. She helped the Prince escape over the sea to Skye in a small boat, with him disguised as her maid. History has made a lot of her. The maid costume has got a lot of press, too.
Mind, the castle was the courthouse for years. Everyone still looks up at it nervously. It's the sandstone. It looks like it knows what you did.

then.text: A drop of rain never stopped a ceilidh. We just dance faster to keep warm. Strip the Willow, anyone?
Mind the midges this time of night. They love a Highland evening almost as much as we do.
Ceilidh's on at the hall. If you can count to eight and spin, you can dance. Even if you can't, really.

ceilidh_dad.text: Fàilte to Inverness! We say 'Inbhir Nis' in Gaelic. It means 'mouth of the Ness', which tells you where to look if you're lost: downhill, towards the sea.
The Keeper's at the ice rink. Isla's a curler. If she says 'hurry hard', do as you're told. She's got a stone and a broom, and she knows how to use both.

gate_inverness.text: Closed for "seasonal rebranding". Skye and the Cairngorms, both. Sorry. I'm told it's temporary.
We're told it'll reopen once the Keeper at the ice rink has had a word with you. Up the hill, on the river. Ice rinks don't hide.

inverness_astronomer.text: This far north the skies get properly dark. On a good night you'll see the Milky Way right over the Ness.
Keep an eye on the north. If it goes green and wavy, that's the aurora. If it goes green and quacks, it's a duck.
I've spent forty winters looking up. Still haven't seen the same night twice.

inverness_fox_watcher.text: Foxes walk the riverbank at night, quiet as anything. Red torch, still feet, and patience.
I saw a pine marten once, right on that wall. Rarer than a dry August. I was grinning for a week.
